Ahead of the White Friday Protest at the EDSA Shrine, Akbayan Partylist reiterated its call for Congress to remove all Unprogrammed Appropriations from the 2026 National Budget.

The House of Representatives is expected to approve the General Appropriations Bill today on 2nd Reading, amid Akbayan’s warning that the ₱43 billion fund risks becoming a black hole for corruption if left unchecked and urged lawmakers to demonstrate genuine commitment to transparency and accountability.

“₱243 billion ang pondong nakatago sa Unprogrammed Allocations. Karapatan ng taumbayan na malaman kung saan mapupunta ang kanilang binabayad na buwis,” said Akbayan President Rafaela David. “Ang Unprogrammed Allocation ay parang ‘secret pocket’ ng gobyerno na pinopondohan ng taumbayan. Hindi malinaw kung para kanino at para saan ang pondo, at pwede nilang paghugutan ng pera kung kailan at para saan nila gusto.”

data.text:
Good morning everyone,

A powerful magnitude 7.4 earthquake has struck off the southern coast of the Philippines, triggering tsunami warnings across parts of the Philippines and neighbouring Indonesia. It’s been an incredibly tense night for residents across the region, many of whom were woken by the violent shaking and urged to move inland immediately.

Authorities warned that waves over a metre high (around 3.3ft) could hit coastal areas a terrifying prospect for communities already used to the constant threat of typhoons and tremors. Coastal towns in the central and southern Philippines have been evacuated as a precaution, with emergency services racing against time to reach isolated areas.

Sadly, there are now confirmed reports of fatalities and injuries, along with widespread power cuts and damaged infrastructure. The images below  taken in Davao Oriental  show the sheer force of the quake, with cracked roads, collapsed walls, and frightened residents standing in disbelief at the destruction around them.

This disaster comes barely a week after another deadly quake struck Cebu province, killing at least 74 people and injuring hundreds more. To suffer back-to-back earthquakes of this strength is truly devastating, and it’s left many Filipinos reeling.

Local journalists on the ground describe chaotic scenes  patients being treated in car parks after hospitals were damaged, and crowds gathering outside emergency centres for news of missing loved ones. One witness, Richie Diuyen, who works for the local disaster agency in Manay, described how the tremor caused students to faint and left many people feeling dizzy and disoriented.

These earthquakes are caused by the Philippines’ location along the Pacific “Ring of Fire”  one of the most seismically active regions on Earth, where several tectonic plates meet and grind together, building up enormous underground pressure. Sadly, it’s also one of the world’s most densely populated coastal zones, which makes the impact of every quake even more severe.

🌏 For now, authorities are still monitoring aftershocks and possible tsunami waves. Rescue and recovery efforts are under way, with emergency teams working through the night.

Our thoughts are with everyone affected by this powerful earthquake. 🙏💔

More updates soon,
KWT Dave

CSAFP’S CORNER | EIGHT YEARS AFTER MARAWI: THE COURAGE THAT REBUILT HOPE

Eight years ago, an important city in Mindanao became the battleground for our nation’s soul. The Battle of Marawi was not just a war against terror but a test of faith, unity, and the Filipino spirit.

In his latest Inquirer column, The General Idea, AFP Chief of Staff General Romeo S. Brawner Jr. revisits this defining chapter that shaped both the Armed Forces and his own calling as a soldier.

At the time of the siege, then-Colonel Brawner was completing his studies at the U.S. Army War College. From a world away, he watched with disbelief as Marawi — a city he knew for its warmth, culture, and faith — was engulfed by darkness.

In that moment, he made a vow: “When I return home, I will go where I’m needed most.”

Upon returning to the Philippines, he went straight to then AFP Chief of Staff General Eduardo Año. Before he could even volunteer, he was told to “Report to Marawi.”

That was all he needed to hear.
As Deputy Commander of Task Force Ranao, he helped protect civilians, secure the outskirts, and keep governance alive amid the ruins. Later, as Commander of the 103rd Infantry Brigade, he led the operation that neutralized Abu Dar—the last Maute–ISIS leader—closing a dark chapter in Philippine history.

But for General Brawner, Marawi was never just a battlefield.

It was a turning point—for the AFP, for the people, and for himself.

He still carries with him the names of the 168 soldiers who made the ultimate sacrifice, especially Captain Rommel Sandoval and PFC Gener Tinangag.

“Their stories remind us that we salute not only with our hands, but with our hearts,” he reflects.

He also witnessed the slow but steady rebirth of Marawi, from families rebuilding homes to children returning to classrooms, and prayers once again echoing from the mosques.

For him, this is the real victory — that peace can grow where war once stood.

Now, as Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, General Brawner shares with us that true strength lies not only in courage under fire but in compassion after the smoke clears.

“Today, and every day after, we must keep building a future where no Filipino child ever learns the sound of war before the sound of morning prayer.”

Marawi stands as a symbol of sacrifice, service, and the enduring will of a nation that refuses to surrender its hope.

data.text:
China  plays a central role in the global fentanyl problem by acting as the primary source of the chemical precursors used to  manufacture the drug.

Following increased regulation of finished  fentanyl products in China, the supply chain shifted to sending  precursor chemicals to Mexico, where cartels complete the manufacturing  process and traffic the final product, especially into the west including the US, Canada, Australia and now EU.  Chinese Fentanyl smugglers were recently caught in both the Philippines and Japan.

The vast pharmaceutical and chemical industries in China are the main global source of the precursor chemicals required to produce illicit fentanyl.  When China restricted the manufacturing and export of finished fentanyl products in 2019, illicit producers in the country shifted their business to producing precursor chemicals instead.

The Chinese government provides subsidies for the production and export of  fentanyl precursors through tax incentives, even though these substances  are prohibited under both US and Chinese law.  PRC state-owned companies, including a government-operated prison, possess ownership interests in firms involved in drug trafficking.

Chinese officials intentionally hindering US law enforcement initiatives.  In several instances, Chinese  authorities purportedly informed fentanyl manufacturers about American  investigations, enabling them to escape prosecution.

While the primary route now involves Mexican cartels, Chinese manufacturers have also been known to ship illicit substances directly to international customers, using tactics to conceal the contents and evade law enforcement.

Despite having a highly monitored internet, Chinese companies openly advertise and sell these illicit materials online. Investigations have found that the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) appears to censor content for domestic drug sales but not for exports. 

Mexican cartels like the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) receive precursor chemicals from China and then manufacture the illicit fentanyl in clandestine labs.

The proceeds from this illegal drug trade are often laundered through Chinese organized criminal groups, which have become a dominant force in global money laundering.   Chinese companies and large banks have been caught laundering money for the Cartels and criminal groups.
